title: Chapter IV

teacherSummary.text: Gatsby drives Nick to the city, telling him a polished life story (Oxford, wealthy dead parents, war medals) and showing proof. At lunch he introduces Meyer Wolfshiem, who fixed the 1919 World Series. Jordan then tells Nick that in 1917 in Louisville, Daisy loved a young officer named Gatsby; she married Tom in 1919 after a night of crying over a letter. Gatsby bought his house to be across the bay from Daisy and wants Nick to invite her to tea.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Nick himself describes a car of Black passengers with racist language and caricature ('two bucks and a girl'), and draws Wolfshiem with antisemitic stereotypes. These are the narrator's words, not a villain's. Do not read the slurs aloud; discuss how they complicate Nick's claim to reserve judgment. Nick's party list mentions Henry L. Palmetto, 'who killed himself by jumping in front of a subway train'. It is said in passing; acknowledge it, use the safe-messaging script, and do not dwell on the method. This section mentions drinking or a drug (“…id the young ladies, moving somewhere between his cocktails and his flowers. “One time he killed a…”). Treat it as period custom or plot detail; name it plainly and don't glamorize it.
contentNotes.studentPreview: The narrator uses racist and antisemitic stereotypes in this chapter. A guest list mentions a man who died by suicide. Support is available if this is hard to read.
